versions.text:
The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, and a skin of ice still clung to the face, but the hands moved freely when he tried them. The weight cable sat snug on its drum among the gears. Then he lifted out a pin from the escapement, a part the size of a grain of rice. It had worn through.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, the cheapest at a cost that made two members wince. Someone raised my grandfather's safety on the ladder, and he laughed. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, barely glanced at the catalogue. The spring fair was three weeks away, she said, and every fair in Orlen Cross opened with the bell ringing noon. She asked only whether he could have it ready by then, and the vote gave him until the fair.

For nine evenings he worked with a file and a rod of steel, his notebook open to a drawing he had made of the escapement in 1983, every part measured to a tenth of a millimetre. I held the lamp and handed him the file when he reached for it. On the morning of the fair he fitted the new pin, and at noon the clock struck twelve over a square full of people.

I still think of his hands that week, bent over that grain of steel, and of the whole square going quiet at the first stroke. It was the finest work I have ever watched anyone do, and he did it at our kitchen table with a file.

The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, and a skin of ice still clung to the face, but the hands moved freely when he tried them. Every pin in the escapement was sound; he had renewed each worn part the spring before. Then he shone his torch down the shaft beside the gears. The weight cable had slipped off its drum and lay in coils on the floor below.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, had borrowed my grandfather's notebook, and she read from it aloud: every repair since 1983, each with its cost, totalled at the foot of the page in her red ink. Someone mentioned the spring fair, three weeks off, and someone else my grandfather's safety on the ladder. Petra read out the total again, and the vote went six to one to replace the old works with Jonas's cheapest model.

Before the meeting closed, Petra struck the keeper's wage from the town accounts, eleven pounds a month that he had drawn since before I was born. Nobody asked him about it. Jonas fitted his grey box beside the old gears the next week and handed my grandfather the old pendulum.

The clock keeps good time now, and the bell rings on the hour. Petra Vell turned forty-one years of his Sundays into a column of figures and then voted him out of a job in the same hour, while the council sat and let her. It was wrong, and at the fair I told her so to her face.

The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, and the weight cable sat snug on its drum among the gears. He tested each pin in the escapement and found every part sound. Then he leaned out through the louvres. Ice had formed on the face overnight, and its weight had bent both hands back against the numerals.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, and spoke of their cost and their safety. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, had stood in the square that morning and watched a man of seventy go up an iron ladder glazed with ice. She asked my grandfather to stay off the tower until someone younger could be trained to keep it. Someone raised the spring fair, three weeks off, and the vote went her way regardless.

No one younger came forward. On the night of the fair a storm took the power, and my grandfather struck a match at the kitchen table and lit the lamp, then sat beside it until late with the tower key in his lap, turning it over and over in his fingers.

In May he handed his notebook to me and asked me to keep it. The hands of the clock still stand at ten past four, bent a little toward the five, and the Harl bus leaves by the driver's watch now. Some mornings I stop in the square and think of that March day, when I might have offered to climb in his place, and of every hour the bell has missed since.

The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. That weekend he had been at his sister's, and before he left he handed me the key. On Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, a skin of ice still clung to the face, and the hands moved freely when he tried them. Every pin and part of the escapement was sound, and the weight cable sat on its drum among the gears. He took out his notebook, where every winding since 1983 had a line and a date, and turned to the last page. The line for Sunday was blank. I had spent that day at a friend's house, with the key in my coat.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, at a cost that would need a vote. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, spoke first about the Harl bus. Its driver set off by the tower clock, and that morning he had left forty minutes late with half the school aboard. She asked how soon the clock could be trusted again. My grandfather said by morning, and someone asked about his safety on the ladder.

Petra struck a bargain with me before the meeting closed. I would wind the clock every Sunday until the end of term, at two pounds a week, and my grandfather would check my work. I wound it that night, and it started at once.

The spring fair opened three weeks later with the bell ringing noon. I wound the clock each Sunday, and Petra paid me what she had agreed. In June the key went back to my grandfather. I spent the summer stacking paint tins at Jonas Brede's shop.

The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. A skin of ice still clung to the face, but the hands moved freely when he tried them, the weight cable sat snug on its drum, and every pin and part of the escapement was sound. Then he lifted his lamp to the gears. Two pigeons had built a nest of twigs and bus tickets between the teeth of the great wheel, and two eggs sat in it, looking thoroughly at home.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, and had already bolted a scaffold to the tower. He spoke of their low cost and of my grandfather's safety on the ladder. Petra Vell, who chaired the council and keeps a bird feeder in every window, had borrowed my grandfather's notebook. She read out an entry from 1991: pigeons in the great wheel, April, left until fledged. Then she read it again and called the vote.

The council voted six to one to leave the nest and its birds where they were. Jonas struck his scaffold the next morning, pole by pole, and stacked the poles in his van, while a small crowd on the bakery steps offered him advice.

For most of April the clock said ten past four. The Harl bus ran by the driver's watch, the spring fair opened to a cheer where the bell should have been, and people took to asking one another the time, which led to a great deal of conversation. In May the chicks flew, and my grandfather swept out the twigs and wound the clock. He handed the bus tickets to the driver, who swore one was his.
